title: The labels and models used to describe problematic substance use impact discrete elements of stigma: A registered report

claims.statement: In one pre-registered online experiment with adults who had no personal or close-family history of substance use or psychiatric diagnoses, the words used to describe a person's difficulty changed some of the attitudes readers reported, but not others, and did not reliably change a pretend money task. 1,613 adults (largest age group 18 to 25; 55.9% women; 77.1% White; recruited through a university participation scheme, Prolific and social media; country of residence not stated) were each randomly assigned to read one short story about a person called Alex. When Alex's serious trouble at home and work was said to come from increasing drug use rather than from a health concern (819 against 741 readers), readers reported wanting more social distance from Alex (standardized difference d 0.87), saw Alex as more dangerous (d 0.78) and gave higher public-stigma scores (d 0.95; means 50.6 against 42.2), large differences by the usual standard; they agreed less that the condition had genetic or disease causes (d −0.35), and their hope for Alex's recovery was the same within the study's equivalence bounds (d −0.06). Among readers of the drug-use story, calling the condition a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' (392 against 423) made readers agree more that it had genetic or disease causes (d 0.54; the study calls this subscale blame), while its effects on social distance (d −0.20), danger (−0.11), hope (−0.07) and public stigma (−0.18) were small and inconclusive, so the study could not tell whether they were more than trivial; on the means, the brain-disease label went with slightly less social distance and public stigma. In a pretend task in which readers could give or take small sums of money for Alex's answers, neither the drug-use description nor the brain-disease label reliably changed what they gave or took, and describing Alex's treatment as likely to succeed rather than uncertain gave only inconclusive differences (Pennington et al., 2023). The study measured attitudes reported after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, health workers or services; it left out people with lived experience; in the drug-use version four questionnaire items named opioids, so that comparison changed the questions as well as the story; the intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals; and it did not compare person-first words with labels for the person. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), a randomized study of two commonly used terms for people with substance-related conditions, is not yet read. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Pennington et al. (2023), Cohen's d with intervals printed as 99% that match 98% intervals (card reporting issue): drug use vs health concern (819 vs 741): social distance 0.87 (0.74 to 0.99), perceived danger 0.78 (0.66 to 0.90), public stigma 0.95 (0.82 to 1.07; means 50.59 vs 42.15), blame subscale (genetic or disease attribution) −0.35 (−0.47 to −0.23), all meaningful by the study's rule; prognostic optimism −0.06 (equivalent); continued care 0.09 (inconclusive); reward −0.03 (equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence); punishment 0.14 (0.02 to 0.26; inconclusive). 'Chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem' (392 vs 423, drug-use arm): blame subscale 0.54 (0.38 to 0.71; means 8.61 vs 7.22), meaningful; continued care 0.01 (equivalent); social distance −0.20 (−0.36 to −0.03), prognostic optimism −0.07, danger −0.11, public stigma −0.18 (−0.34 to −0.02; means 49.62 vs 51.20) and reward 0.15, all inconclusive; punishment 0.007 (equivalent). Treatment framed as likely to succeed vs uncertain (383 vs 362): every self-report measure and reward inconclusive (for example public stigma 0.31, 0.14 to 0.48, higher with the uncertain framing), punishment equivalent. Detectable equivalence bounds ±0.28 and ±0.30 for the label and treatment comparisons.
